summary: Hong Kong is legal for keeping a pet roof rat but has no lawful pathway to bring one in from outside. AFCD confirmed in writing (8 July 2026, Import and Export Division) that the department does not regulate the keeping of rats, so a domesticated Rattus rattus needs no keeping licence, and Rattus rattus is not protected wildlife (the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance, Cap. 170). The hard wall is import: because R. rattus is a designated rodent-control pest, AFCD stated it will NOT issue an import permit for it as a domesticated pet (an advance permit under Cap. 139 and Cap. 421 is otherwise required, and importing without one is an offence). Private, non-commercial breeding is unregulated and giving a pet's offspring away free is unregulated, but commercial sale runs into a catch: a licensed animal-trade premises (Cap. 139B) must run a mammalian-pest control programme, so selling or keeping R. rattus on licensed premises may contradict its own licence. A public-health overlay remains: the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department treats all rodents as 'vermin' under Cap. 132, enforced on a complaint/infestation basis rather than against sanitarily-caged pets. Net: legal to keep, but source it locally, since there is no pet-import pathway.

keep.why: AFCD confirmed in writing (8 July 2026, Import and Export Division): 'This Department does not regulate the keeping of rats', so keeping a domesticated Rattus rattus needs no keeping licence. Consistent with the prior finding that R. rattus is not a protected wild animal (the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance, Cap. 170). One overlay remains outside AFCD's remit: the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance (Cap. 132, s.47) defines all rodents as 'vermin', a duty the FEHD enforces on a complaint/infestation basis (elimination notices, not raids on sanitarily-caged pets).
keep.governing_law: Cap. 170 Sch. 2 (wildlife, Muridae omitted); AFCD 8 Jul 2026 reply (keeping of rats not regulated); Cap. 132 s.47 (FEHD 'vermin' duty).

breed.why: Private, non-commercial breeding is unregulated: Hong Kong created dedicated breeder licences only for dogs (Cap. 139B), leaving small mammals unregulated at the breeding stage. AFCD noted (8 July 2026) that a licensed animal-trade premises must run a mammalian-pest control and destruction programme, so keeping or breeding R. rattus on LICENSED (commercial) premises may contradict that licence, but this bites only at the commercial tier; hobbyist breeding of a kept pet is not licensed and is unaffected.
breed.governing_law: Cap. 139B (dog breeder licences only; small mammals unregulated at private breeding; the licensed-premises pest-control duty bites only commercially).

sell_give.why: Giving a pet's offspring away free (no consideration) is unregulated, and a statutory hobbyist exemption covers selling an animal 'kept by him as a pet or any offspring thereof' (Cap. 139B s.4). Commercial sale 'by way of business' needs an Animal Trader Licence, but AFCD noted (8 July 2026) that a licensed premises must run a mammalian-pest control programme, so selling or keeping R. rattus on licensed premises 'may contradict' that requirement. Practical effect: free and hobbyist rehoming is fine; a formal commercial trade in R. rattus runs against its own licence.
sell_give.governing_law: Cap. 139B s.4 (Animal Trader Licence + pet/offspring hobbyist exemption; the licensed-premises mammalian-pest-control duty conflicts with a commercial R. rattus trade).

transport.why: This record encodes the IMPORT position, which is the binding hard rule. AGENCY-CONFIRMED (AFCD, 8 July 2026, Import and Export Division): AFCD 'will not issue an import permit for [Rattus rattus] importation for domesticated pet purpose' because R. rattus is a designated rodent-control pest. An advance import permit under the Public Health (Animals and Birds) Ordinance (Cap. 139) and the Rabies Ordinance (Cap. 421) is otherwise required for any mammal, and importing without one is an offence, but for a pet R. rattus that permit will not be granted, so there is no lawful pet-import pathway. Internal movement of a lawfully-kept pet within Hong Kong is unencumbered (subject only to the humane-transport duty, Cap. 169). Never release into the wild.
transport.governing_law: Cap. 139 s.5 + Cap. 421 (advance import permit required; AFCD will not issue it for a pet R. rattus); Cap. 169 (humane transport).

restrictions.summary: Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is lawful in Hong Kong, but there is NO pet-import pathway: AFCD confirmed (8 July 2026) it will not issue an import permit for R. rattus as a domesticated pet (designated rodent-control pest). Commercial sale needs an Animal Trader Licence, whose mandatory mammalian-pest-control programme conflicts with trading R. rattus, so the practical route is local captive-bred stock and hobbyist/free rehoming. Keep proof your rat is captive-bred (re: the Cap. 132 'vermin' duty). Never release.
steps: Source a pet from local captive-bred stock (no lawful pet-import permit is available)
For free rehoming, no licence is needed; commercial sale needs an Animal Trader Licence, which conflicts with the licensed-premises pest-control duty
restrictions.fees: Import permit HK$432 first animal + HK$102 each additional

inquiry_focus: (1) Does AFCD's suspension of commercial (unaccompanied) rodent imports apply equally to a private hobbyist importing one or two personally-accompanied captive-bred Rattus rattus as pets, or can a Special Permit (Form AF240) still issue for non-commercial personal rodent import? (2) Does AFCD or any HK authority interpret s.47 of Cap. 132 (the vermin-elimination duty) as applying to lawfully-kept captive-bred pet rats in a private dwelling, or only to feral/commensal infestation? (3) What is AFCD's position on the threshold between 'private breeding' (no ATL) and 'trading/breeding by way of business' under Cap. 139B for a hobbyist who rehomes occasional litters at no charge?
